extracted_claims.text: Article 43 of the AI Act sets out the conformity assessment procedures that providers of high-risk AI systems must follow before placing them on the market or putting them into service.

For high-risk AI systems listed in point 1 of Annex III (biometrics), where the provider has applied harmonised standards (Article 40) or common specifications (Article 41), the provider may choose between internal control (Annex VI) or an assessment involving a notified body (Annex VII).
The provider must follow the Annex VII (notified body) procedure where harmonised standards do not exist or the provider has not fully applied them.

For high-risk AI systems listed in points 2 to 8 of Annex III (covering employment, education, essential services, law enforcement, migration, and justice), only self-assessment under Annex VI applies; no notified body is required.

Annex VI (internal control) requires the provider to verify its own quality management system, examine technical documentation, and confirm design, development and post-market monitoring processes are consistent with that documentation, without third-party involvement.

Annex VII (notified body assessment) involves a two-stage third-party process: assessment of the quality management system and assessment of the technical documentation, followed by ongoing surveillance of the approved system.

For high-risk AI systems already covered by existing EU product legislation listed in Annex I (Section A), providers must follow the relevant sectoral conformity assessment procedures, with notified bodies verifying compliance with AI-specific requirements; classification as high-risk does not itself mandate third-party assessment if the sectoral legislation allows reliance on harmonised standards or common specifications.

Under Article 46, a market surveillance authority may, by way of derogation from Article 43 and upon a duly justified request, authorise the placing on the market or putting into service of specific high-risk AI systems for a limited time, for exceptional reasons of public security, protection of life and health, environmental protection, or protection of key industrial and infrastructural assets.

A 2023 consolidated draft text of the AI Act (dated 11 May 2023) stated that for systems put into service by law enforcement, immigration or asylum authorities, or EU institutions, bodies or agencies, the competent market surveillance authority (under Article 63(5) or (6)) would act as the notified body, and that for other high-risk systems the provider could choose any notified body.

Only conformity assessment bodies that have been formally designated under the AI Act may carry out conformity assessments, and only for the specific types of AI systems within the scope of their designation, as determined by a list of codes and categories.

Notified bodies are designated by Member States and listed in the Commission's NANDO (New Approach Notified and Designated Organisations) database; manufacturers may choose any notified body legally designated to carry out the relevant conformity assessment procedure.
As of March 2026, the notified body ecosystem for AI Act conformity assessment is still being built, with designation processes ongoing across Member States and limited capacity.
As of early 2026, the pool of formally designated notified bodies under the AI Act remains very small.

As of September 2026, sources such as national data protection authorities (BfDI, CNIL, Data Protection Commission) report no notified-body role under the AI Act, while CEN-CENELEC's JTC 21 develops harmonised standards supporting the Act.

Under the related Medical Devices Regulation (MDR) and In Vitro Diagnostic Regulation (IVDR), as of October 2025/February 2026, NANDO listed 51–52 MDR-designated notified bodies and 19 IVDR-designated notified bodies, illustrating the scale of a mature notified body ecosystem in a comparable EU product regime, but these are not AI Act notified bodies.

Under the Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), as of late June 2026, zero notified bodies had been designated in the Commission's NANDO database, with a target of 11 December 2026 for sufficient notified body capacity and full application from 11 December 2027, illustrating a similar slow-start pattern in notified body designation for a comparable new EU regulation.
The EU has not published an official template or standardized methodology for carrying out a conformity assessment under the AI Act, despite requiring one for high-risk systems.

contradictions.claim_a: A 2023 consolidated draft (dated 11 May 2023) of the AI Act specified that for high-risk systems used by law enforcement, immigration, asylum authorities, or EU institutions/bodies/agencies, the relevant market surveillance authority would act as the notified body under Article 63(5) or (6).
contradictions.claim_b: The final consolidated AI Act text (Regulation 2024/1689, version effective 27 July 2026) and other current summaries of Article 43 describe only the internal control (Annex VI) versus notified-body (Annex VII) distinction based on Annex III categories, without referencing market surveillance authorities acting as notified bodies for law enforcement/immigration systems.
contradictions.description: Source 11 reflects an earlier 2023 proposal/consolidated text containing a specific provision (market surveillance authority acting as notified body for law enforcement/immigration/asylum/EU-body systems) that does not appear in the final adopted Article 43 text summarized by sources 13, 26, and 27, suggesting this provision may have been altered or removed between the 2023 draft and the final 2024 Regulation.

open_issues: No source provides a current, comprehensive list or count of notified bodies that have been formally designated specifically under the EU AI Act (as opposed to MDR, IVDR, or CRA notified bodies).

It is unclear whether the 2023 draft provision requiring market surveillance authorities to act as notified bodies for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, and EU institutional AI systems was retained, amended, or removed in the final adopted AI Act text (Regulation 2024/1689).
Sources do not specify exact numbers, names, or Member States of any notified bodies currently designated for AI Act conformity assessment as of October 2026.
It is unclear what concrete capacity-building timeline or targets (analogous to the CRA's 11 December 2026 target) apply to AI Act notified body designation.
The sources do not clarify how the Article 46 derogation procedure interacts with or affects conformity assessment timelines once a notified body ecosystem matures.

It is unclear whether harmonised standards referenced in Article 40 have been finalized, which would affect whether Annex VI or Annex VII procedures apply in practice for Annex III point 1 (biometric) systems.
report:
# Conformity Assessment Procedures for High-Risk AI Systems Under the EU AI Act

## Executive Summary
Article 43 of the EU AI Act establishes a dual-track conformity assessment regime for high-risk AI systems, allowing either internal control (Annex VI) or third-party assessment by a notified body (Annex VII), with the applicable route depending on the Annex III category and whether harmonised standards exist (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727), [AI Act Law](https://ai-act-law.eu/article/43)). However, the notified body ecosystem specifically designated under the AI Act appears nascent or largely undocumented, with no source providing a current, verifiable list of AI Act-designated notified bodies (low confidence).

## Key Findings

### Legal Framework for Conformity Assessment
Article 43 of the AI Act sets out the conformity assessment procedures providers of high-risk AI systems must follow before market placement or deployment (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727), [Artificial Intelligence Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43)). For Annex III point 1 systems (biometrics), providers may choose between internal control (Annex VI) or notified body assessment (Annex VII) where harmonised standards (Article 40) or common specifications (Article 41) have been applied (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727), [DPO Consulting](https://www.dpo-consulting.com/blog/ai-conformity-assessment)). Where harmonised standards do not exist or have not been fully applied, the Annex VII notified-body procedure becomes mandatory (high confidence) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727), [Artificial Intelligence Act](https://artificialintelligenceact.eu/article/43)).

A low-confidence claim suggests that for Annex III points 2–8 systems (employment, education, essential services, law enforcement, migration, and justice), only self-assessment under Annex VI applies with no notified body requirement ([Deeploy](https://deeploy.ai/eu-ai-act-hub/articles/eu-ai-act-conformity-self-assessment-vs-notified-body-review-explained)); this claim warrants caution given its single-source, low-authority basis.

Annex VI internal control requires providers to verify their own quality management system and technical documentation without third-party involvement (high confidence) ([Regumatrix](https://regumatrix.eu/compliance/conformity-assessment), [JRC](https://publications.jrc.ec.europa.eu/repository/bitstream/JRC132833/JRC132833_01.pdf)). Annex VII involves a two-stage third-party process—assessment of the quality management system and technical documentation—followed by ongoing surveillance (high confidence) ([Regumatrix](https://regumatrix.eu/compliance/conformity-assessment), [EU AI Act Blog](https://www.euaiact.com/blog/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment)).

For systems already covered by Annex I Section A sectoral legislation (e.g., medical devices, machinery), providers follow existing sectoral procedures, with notified bodies verifying AI-specific requirements only where sectoral rules require third-party assessment (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-43)). Article 46 permits market surveillance authorities to authorise limited exceptions to Article 43 for public security, health, environmental, or infrastructure reasons (medium confidence) ([AI Act Service Desk](https://ai-act-service-desk.ec.europa.eu/en/ai-act/article-46)).

Only formally designated conformity assessment bodies may conduct assessments, limited to the specific AI system types within their designation scope (medium confidence) ([Council document](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-7322-2026-INIT/en/pdf)).

### Notified Body Designation Status
Notified bodies are designated by Member States and listed in the Commission's NANDO database, with manufacturers free to choose any legally designated body (high confidence) ([European Commission](https://single-market-economy.ec.europa.eu/single-market/goods/building-blocks/notified-bodies_en)). However, low-confidence sources indicate the AI Act notified body ecosystem remains small and still under construction as of early-to-mid 2026, with ongoing designation processes and limited capacity across Member States ([eyreACT](https://eyreact.com/notified-bodies-ai-act), [LinkedIn analysis](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/eu-ai-act-conformity-assessment-what-providers-must-do-zunic-maric-0dfof)). One low-confidence source reports that as of September 2026, national data protection authorities indicate no notified-body role has materialized under the AI Act, while CEN-CENELEC's JTC 21 continues developing supporting harmonised standards ([Optinest](https://optinest.de/ai-infrastructure/regulation/conformity-assessment/notified-body-eu-ai-act-when-third-party-assessment-is-mandatory)).

For comparison, the mature MDR/IVDR regime has 51–52 and 19 designated notified bodies respectively (high confidence), while the newer CRA had zero designated notified bodies as of June 2026, illustrating a common slow-start pattern for notified body ecosystems under new EU product regulations (both low-to-high confidence, depending on source) ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A52025SC1051), [CyberCertLabs](https://www.cybercertlabs.com/case-studies/insights-cra-notified-bodies-2026)).

## Contradictions & Uncertainties
A 2023 consolidated draft text stated that market surveillance authorities would act as notified bodies for law enforcement, immigration, asylum, and EU institutional AI systems ([European Parliament, 2023](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/meetdocs/2014_2019/plmrep/COMMITTEES/CJ40/DV/2023/05-11/ConsolidatedCA_IMCOLIBE_AI_ACT_EN.pdf)); this provision does not appear in the final adopted Article 43 text ([EUR-Lex](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML?uri=CELEX%3A02024R1689-20260727)), suggesting it was altered or removed—**flagged as low confidence (0.17)**. Multiple claims regarding current notified body capacity (confidence 0.12) are flagged as low confidence due to reliance on single, low-authority blog sources. The claim regarding Annex III points 2–8 requiring only self-assessment (0.12) is similarly uncertain and may oversimplify the actual legal position.

## Knowledge Gaps
No source provides a current, verified list or count of notified bodies formally designated specifically under the AI Act. It remains unclear whether the 2023 draft's market-surveillance-authority provision was retained in the final Regulation. Exact capacity-building timelines for AI Act notified body designation, and the finalization status of Article 40 harmonised standards (which determines Annex VI vs. VII applicability for biometric systems), are not documented in available sources.
